summary:
Ceará stands under Brazil's national framework for LGBTI people: the Constitution, the Penal Code and federal anti-discrimination provisions apply uniformly in the state, and there is no state-level legal distinction governing gender identity or expression. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, the age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation, and an expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's documents and family status are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry.

After the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling, constitutional and federal criminal provisions prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism. Courts have applied these provisions to commercial conduct: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing. Protection machinery has also widened, with lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, bringing trans people within the country's violence-prevention statutes.

Ceará's record on violence runs against that protective text. A G1/Globo report of 28 January 2025, citing the ANTRA dossier, records that Ceará was the Northeast state with the most killings of trans people in 2024, with 11 killings, the third-highest count nationally. The ninth ANTRA dossier, reported in January 2026, again places Ceará among the states with the most trans killings in 2025, with 8 cases; a national television network's account of the same dossier has Ceará tied at the top of the 2025 state ranking with another state, on 8 killings each. Nationally the 2025 total was 80, a 34% reduction against 2024, but still the highest in the world for an eighteenth consecutive year; 1,261 trans people were killed between 2017 and 2025, an average of 140 a year. Of the 57 victims with race data in 2025, 70% were Black, against a 77% average for the 2017–2025 period.

National conditions explain the ranking. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions. A May 2024 investigation documented 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife. In the October 2024 municipal elections, close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of the country and received death threats and intimidation, while the number of trans officeholders tripled against the previous cycle.

Detention carries a specific regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. On arrest the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person has been consulted about their preference; the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, a later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census of travestis and transgender women held in Rio de Janeiro state prisons between April and June 2021 interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in the metropolitan region; it documents housing in units operated as masculine, with some held in so-called neutral or security units, and treats placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. A 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law grants parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics, and national norms from 2014 and 2020 permit people to be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine. No Ceará-specific source in this inventory describes how the state's own prison system applies these national rules.
tangentialFactors:
The national homicide tally has moved in the right direction and against the direction of Ceará's own position: the 2025 national total fell 34% year on year while Ceará remained at or near the top of the state ranking in both 2024 and 2025. A visitor's exposure is therefore better predicted by the state-level figure than by the national one.

International placement norms for trans prisoners are more clearly articulated in some other systems than Brazil's general practice. A general-encyclopaedia overview of LGBTQ people in prison sets out Scotland's 2022 inspection standards, under which trans and intersex prisoners are admitted to facilities matching their lived or experienced gender, and Canadian practice of placing prisoners by gender identity. Those comparisons describe other jurisdictions; they do not bind Ceará's authorities.

Racial dimension: two-thirds or more of trans homicide victims with available race data are Black in every recent year cited, so violence in Ceará is not distributed evenly across the trans population.
localsOnly:
Residents inside the prison system hold entitlements that depend on where they are held. The 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law grants travestis and trans women in women's units parity of treatment with cisgender women on hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics; that law governs Rio de Janeiro state prisons, not Ceará's. National norms from 2014 and 2020 permit people to be housed according to their choice, including in units denominated masculine.

Rights on paper include the right of transgender people to be referred to by their social name rather than their birth name and to be forwarded to women's prisons, and the right of LGBTQ prisoners to choose male or female clothing. These statements appear in a general-encyclopaedia article on LGBT rights in Brazil whose underlying citation is a 2012 interview archived in January 2012.

Political participation by trans residents has risen sharply: the number of trans officeholders tripled in the October 2024 municipal cycle, even as close to 1,000 trans candidates nationally reported death threats and intimidation.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: a general-encyclopaedia overview (updated 28 September 2026) reports no codified Brazil-specific trans-prisoner housing policy, describing only traumatic social vulnerability and stigma facing travestis and transgender people in rehabilitation. This directly conflicts with the National Council of Justice Resolutions 348 and 366 in this dossier, which are codified national rules; the encyclopedia's Brazil paragraph appears not to reflect them. The resolutions are the better-sourced statement of the current rule.

Unresolved: the encyclopaedia's claims about social-name use, transfer to women's prisons and clothing choice are footnoted to a single archived interview from 2012 and predate Resolutions 348 and 366. Current enforcement in Ceará's own prison system is not sourced in this inventory.

Unresolved: race data was available for 57 of the 80 victims recorded nationally in 2025, so the racial profile of that year's victims rests on a partial count. The inventory gives no Ceará-specific breakdown by race.

Not sourced in this inventory: any Ceará state or municipal ordinance specific to gender identity or expression; any documented case of a trans visitor being refused entry, screened or detained at a Ceará port of entry; and any hate-crime prosecution in Ceará under the 2019 framework.
